stem: A media company serves a CloudFront distribution with an S3 origin for video segments and a second cache behavior for /api/* that forwards to an ALB origin returning personalized data. The API response varies only by a sessionId query string parameter, but many other tracking query strings are appended by the client. The team wants to maximize the cache hit ratio for the /api/* behavior while still personalizing correctly. What should they configure?

choices.text: Create a cache policy for the /api/* behavior that forwards all query strings to the origin
Create a cache policy for the /api/* behavior that includes only the sessionId query string parameter in the cache key
Attach an origin request policy that forwards the User-Agent and Referer headers instead of query strings
Disable caching entirely for the /api/* behavior and forward every request to the origin

explanation: Scoping the cache key to only the sessionId parameter lets CloudFront cache one object per unique session while ignoring the extraneous tracking parameters, maximizing hit ratio. Forwarding all query strings (A) would fragment the cache into near-unique objects per request, and disabling caching (D) removes any performance benefit even though it would technically be correct behavior-wise.

stem: A gaming company is building a real-time multiplayer title that uses a custom UDP protocol on a fixed set of ports. Clients need a small set of static anycast IP addresses to hardcode into the game client, and traffic must fail over to healthy endpoints in another Region within seconds if a Region becomes impaired. There is no HTTP traffic and no need for content caching. Which edge networking service best fits this requirement?

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront with a custom origin
AWS Global Accelerator
Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing
Application Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing

explanation: Global Accelerator provides static anycast IP addresses and supports both TCP and UDP traffic with health-check-driven failover at the network layer, independent of DNS TTLs, making it ideal for non-HTTP, low-latency, fast-failover use cases like real-time gaming. CloudFront (A) is designed for HTTP/HTTPS content delivery and caching, not raw UDP game traffic.

stem: A company runs a public-facing application on an Application Load Balancer in a single AWS Region and does not use CloudFront. Security requires that Layer 7 protections such as SQL injection and rate-based rules be enforced directly on the load balancer. Which AWS WAF configuration is required?

choices.text: A WAF Web ACL with scope CLOUDFRONT, deployed in us-east-1
A WAF Web ACL with scope REGIONAL, created in the same Region as the ALB and associated with the ALB
AWS Shield Advanced enabled on the ALB, which automatically applies WAF managed rules
A WAF Web ACL associated with the VPC route table in front of the ALB

explanation: Regional resources such as an ALB, API Gateway REST API, or AppSync API require a REGIONAL-scope Web ACL created in the same Region as the resource; CLOUDFRONT-scope Web ACLs (A) can only be associated with CloudFront distributions and must be created in us-east-1. Shield Advanced (C) provides DDoS protection and cost protection but does not itself apply WAF rules unless a Web ACL is separately associated.

stem: A CloudFront distribution is configured with an origin group containing a primary S3 origin and a secondary S3 origin in another Region for disaster recovery. During a test, the primary bucket is made to return HTTP 403 responses for all objects, but CloudFront continues serving the 403 errors to viewers instead of failing over to the secondary origin. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Origin groups only support ALB and EC2 custom origins, not S3 origins
The origin group's failover criteria does not include the 403 status code
The secondary origin's bucket policy blocks CloudFront's OAC
CloudFront origin groups only fail over based on TCP connection timeouts, never HTTP status codes

explanation: CloudFront origin groups fail over only for the specific HTTP status codes configured in the failover criteria (commonly 500, 502, 503, 504); if 403 was not added to that list, CloudFront treats it as a valid response and does not trigger failover. Origin groups fully support S3 origins (A is false), and while a bucket policy issue (C) is plausible in general, the scenario states 403s are expected from the primary by design, pointing to a failover-criteria gap.

stem: An engineering team needs to call an external third-party fraud-detection API and inspect the response body before forwarding a request to their origin, adding significant per-request latency and requiring outbound network calls from the edge. Which CloudFront edge compute feature should they use, and why can the alternative not be used?

choices.text: CloudFront Functions, because they support outbound network calls to third-party APIs
Lambda@Edge on the origin-request event, because CloudFront Functions cannot make network calls or access the request body from the edge in this way
Lambda@Edge on the viewer-response event only, because origin-request events are not supported
CloudFront Functions on the origin-response event, because they support higher memory and execution time than Lambda@Edge

explanation: Lambda@Edge supports all four CloudFront event types (viewer request/response and origin request/response), longer execution times, more memory, and network access to external services, making it suitable for calling a third-party API. CloudFront Functions are intentionally limited to sub-millisecond, in-memory JavaScript operations on viewer request/response events and cannot make network calls, so they cannot fulfill this requirement.

stem: A game studio wants to expose thousands of backend game server instances behind a small set of static IP addresses, preserve the original client IP address end to end, and map incoming client connections directly to specific instance IP:port combinations without deploying a load balancer in front of the fleet. Which Global Accelerator feature satisfies this?

choices.text: A standard accelerator with a Network Load Balancer endpoint
A custom routing accelerator mapping port ranges to destination instance IP addresses and ports
A standard accelerator with client affinity set to SOURCE_IP
A standard accelerator with an Elastic IP endpoint and health checks disabled

explanation: Custom routing accelerators are purpose-built for this pattern: they deterministically map accelerator IP:port combinations to specific destination instance IP:port combinations without requiring a load balancer, and they can preserve the client's source IP address. Standard accelerators (A, C, D) route to load balancer, EC2, or EIP endpoints and use health checks and flow hashing rather than direct port-to-instance mapping.

stem: A CloudFront distribution has cache behaviors configured in this order: a default behavior (*) that caches based on all headers with a short TTL, followed by a behavior for the path pattern /images/*. Static images under /images/ are being served with the default behavior's short TTL and low cache hit ratio instead of the long-TTL image-optimized behavior. What is the root cause and fix?

choices.text: CloudFront evaluates behaviors in ascending order of specificity automatically, so this should already work
Path pattern behaviors are evaluated in the order listed in the distribution, and the default (*) behavior is always evaluated last, so /images/* must be reordered before the default behavior
The /images/* behavior needs a higher precedence number set explicitly in a separate priority field
CloudFront requires a wildcard at the end of every path pattern, so /images/* is invalid and falling through to default

explanation: CloudFront evaluates cache behaviors in the exact order they appear in the distribution configuration and applies the first path pattern that matches, with the default (*) behavior always evaluated last regardless of position; if /images/* was accidentally placed after the default behavior, requests would incorrectly match the catch-all first only if listed after it, but the real issue described is that specific patterns must be ordered ahead of any catch-all pattern they should take precedence over. There is no separate numeric priority field distinct from list order.

stem: A company has no customers in South America or Australia and wants to reduce CloudFront costs by limiting which edge locations serve their content, while still serving North America, Canada, and Europe with full performance. Which setting should they change, and what is the tradeoff?

choices.text: Set the distribution's Price Class to one that excludes South America and Australia edge locations; users in excluded regions will be served from the nearest included edge location, potentially with higher latency
Enable Origin Shield in a South American Region to reduce cost for that traffic
Restrict the distribution's geographic restriction (geo-blocking) to allow only North America and Europe, which blocks all other users entirely
Reduce the default TTL on all cache behaviors, which lowers the number of edge locations CloudFront uses

explanation: Price Class settings let you choose the set of CloudFront edge locations used to serve content strictly to control cost, and users outside the selected locations are still served, just from the nearest available edge location which may add latency. Geo-restriction (C) is a different feature that blocks access entirely rather than optimizing cost, and TTL settings (D) have no effect on which edge locations are used.

stem: A CloudFront distribution's origin is an on-premises data center reached over Direct Connect. During peak hours, the origin experiences high request volume even though CloudFront edge caches show a reasonable overall hit ratio, because many different edge locations around the world each experience their first cache miss for the same rarely-changing objects and hit the origin independently. Which feature should be enabled to reduce this origin load?

choices.text: Signed URLs with a short expiration
Origin Shield, placed in a Region close to the origin
A second CloudFront distribution pointed at the same origin to split traffic
Field-level encryption on the cache behavior

explanation: Origin Shield adds an additional caching layer between the edge locations and the origin, consolidating cache-miss requests from many edge locations into a single point closer to the origin so the origin sees far fewer duplicate requests. Signed URLs (A) and field-level encryption (D) address access control and data protection, not origin load, and a second distribution (C) would not deduplicate misses and adds operational complexity.

stem: An application team wants to roll out a new backend version to a small percentage of production traffic before a full cutover, gradually increasing the percentage of users sent to the new version over several days. Which Route 53 routing policy is designed for this?

choices.text: Weighted routing policy, adjusting the relative weights of the old and new record sets over time
Failover routing policy with the new version as secondary
Multivalue answer routing policy
Geolocation routing policy

explanation: Weighted routing lets you assign relative weights to multiple records for the same name, controlling what proportion of DNS responses (and therefore traffic) go to each target, which is exactly the mechanism for a gradual canary rollout. Failover (B) is for active/passive disaster recovery, not gradual percentage shifts, and multivalue (C) returns multiple healthy records without weighted control.

stem: A company has application stacks deployed in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. They currently use geolocation routing but want to be able to gradually shift a small, controlled percentage of traffic from one Region to the other for a capacity test, without changing which physical Region actually serves which countries. Which Route 53 capability should they use instead?

choices.text: Geoproximity routing with a bias value, configured through a Traffic Flow policy
Simple routing with two A records for the same name
Geolocation routing with a smaller number of country-level records
Latency-based routing with health checks disabled

explanation: Geoproximity routing (available via Route 53 Traffic Flow) routes traffic based on the geographic location of resources and lets you apply a bias to expand or shrink the geographic region from which traffic is routed to a given resource, enabling fine, controlled shifts of traffic volume. Plain geolocation routing (C) matches strictly on the user's location to a specific record with no mechanism for gradual, weighted shifting.

stem: A company is migrating workloads to a VPC and wants on-premises servers to resolve records hosted in a Route 53 private hosted zone associated with that VPC, without exposing the zone publicly. What should they configure?

choices.text: A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint, and a forwarding rule sending queries for the zone's domain to on-premises DNS servers
A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC, and conditional forwarding on the on-premises DNS servers pointing the private zone's domain to the inbound endpoint's IP addresses
A public hosted zone with the same domain name and NS delegation from the on-premises DNS
AWS Site-to-Site VPN with DNS64 enabled

explanation: A Resolver inbound endpoint provides IP addresses inside the VPC that on-premises DNS servers can forward queries to; combined with conditional forwarding rules on-premises for the private zone's domain, this lets on-premises clients resolve records in the AWS private hosted zone. An outbound endpoint (A) is used for the opposite direction, forwarding queries that originate in the VPC out to on-premises DNS servers.

stem: A company registered its domain with a third-party registrar and hosts its zone in Route 53. They have enabled DNSSEC signing on the hosted zone, which created a customer-managed KSK backed by AWS KMS and Route 53-managed ZSKs. Which additional step is required for validating resolvers to establish the full chain of trust?

choices.text: Nothing further is needed; enabling DNSSEC signing in Route 53 automatically completes the chain of trust
Retrieve the DS record information from Route 53 and add it to the parent zone (domain) at the third-party registrar
Create a CNAME record pointing to the KMS key ARN
Rotate the ZSK manually before the chain of trust can be established

explanation: DNSSEC establishes a chain of trust from the parent zone down; after signing is enabled and a DS (Delegation Signer) record is generated from the KSK, that DS record must be published in the parent zone, which for a domain registered elsewhere means submitting it to the third-party registrar. Route 53 cannot do this automatically because it does not control the parent zone in that case.

stem: A security team wants resources inside a VPC to be blocked from resolving known malicious domains, while allowing an explicit allow-list of approved external domains for API integrations, all enforced at the DNS layer before a connection is even attempted. Which service should they configure?

choices.text: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall with domain list rule groups associated to the VPC
AWS Network Firewall with stateful domain filtering rules only
Security groups with FQDN-based outbound rules
VPC Flow Logs with a Lambda function that terminates matching connections

explanation: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall lets you create domain list rule groups (block, allow, or alert) and associate them with VPCs, blocking or allowing DNS resolution for specified domains before any connection is attempted. Security groups (C) cannot filter by domain name, and Network Firewall (B) can also filter domains but operates on traffic flows rather than at the Resolver query stage, making DNS Firewall the more direct and lower-latency fit described.

stem: A Route 53 failover routing configuration has a primary record with an associated health check and a secondary record. During an incident, the primary endpoint is actually healthy and reachable from the internet, but Route 53 still marks the health check as unhealthy and fails traffic over to the secondary. What is a likely cause to investigate first?

choices.text: The secondary record's TTL is set too low
The primary endpoint's security group does not allow inbound traffic from the Route 53 health checker IP ranges
Failover routing policies do not support health checks on the primary record
The hosted zone is a private hosted zone, which does not support failover routing at all

explanation: Route 53 health checkers originate from a published set of AWS IP ranges; if the primary endpoint's security group or network ACL does not explicitly allow traffic from those ranges, health checks will report unhealthy even though the endpoint is reachable from elsewhere. Failover routing policies fully support and rely on primary health checks (C is false), and TTL (A) affects caching of the answer, not health check evaluation.

stem: A shared services account owns a Route 53 Resolver rule that conditionally forwards queries for corp.example.com to on-premises DNS servers via an outbound endpoint. The rule has been shared with several spoke accounts using AWS RAM. Instances in one spoke VPC still fail to resolve corp.example.com, while instances in another spoke VPC that received the same shared rule resolve it correctly. What configuration step was most likely missed for the failing VPC?

choices.text: The Resolver rule must be associated with the failing VPC in addition to being shared via RAM
RAM sharing does not support Resolver rules, so a duplicate rule must be created in the spoke account
The outbound endpoint needs a separate IP address allocated per consuming VPC
Security groups on the Resolver outbound endpoint must allow traffic from the spoke VPC's CIDR

explanation: Sharing a Resolver rule via RAM only makes it available to be used by other accounts; each VPC that needs to actually use the rule must still have the rule explicitly associated with it. Resolver rules do support RAM sharing (B is false), and outbound endpoint IP allocation and security groups are unrelated to per-VPC rule association.

stem: A team needs simple DNS-based load balancing across up to eight healthy web server IP addresses, with Route 53 automatically excluding any address that fails its health check from the response, but without needing weighted percentage control or a load balancer. Which routing policy fits best?

choices.text: Weighted routing with equal weights on all eight records
Multivalue answer routing policy with a health check on each record
Simple routing with a single record containing multiple values
Latency-based routing across all eight records

explanation: Multivalue answer routing returns up to eight healthy record values selected at random per query, and Route 53 automatically omits any record whose associated health check has failed, giving simple, health-checked DNS-level load distribution. Simple routing (C) can hold multiple values but Route 53 does not perform health checking or omit unhealthy values with simple routing.

stem: Account A owns a Route 53 private hosted zone that needs to be resolvable from a VPC that lives in Account B. What two actions, in order, are required to associate Account B's VPC with Account A's private hosted zone? (Select TWO)

choices.text: In Account A, create a VPC association authorization for Account B's VPC and the hosted zone
In Account B, call the API to associate the VPC with the hosted zone, referencing the hosted zone ID from Account A
In Account B, share the VPC with Account A using AWS RAM before any authorization can be created
In Account A, manually add Account B's VPC CIDR as an allowed network ACL entry on the hosted zone
In Account A, delete and recreate the hosted zone as a shared resource

explanation: Cross-account private hosted zone association requires the hosted zone's owning account to first create a VPC association authorization naming the other account's VPC and hosted zone, after which the VPC-owning account calls AssociateVPCWithHostedZone referencing that hosted zone. Route 53 hosted zones are not shared via RAM (C) and have no network ACL concept (D).

stem: A global application uses Route 53 latency-based routing with records in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. After deploying a new stack in ap-southeast-1, users in Australia continue to be routed to the us-east-1 endpoint even though the new ap-southeast-1 endpoint would provide much lower latency for them. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Latency-based routing requires at least three records before it activates
No latency record was created for the ap-southeast-1 endpoint, so Route 53 can only choose the lowest latency among the existing us-east-1 and eu-west-1 records
Latency-based routing always prefers the first record created regardless of measured latency
Australian resolvers are cached and require a Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule to be cleared

explanation: Route 53 selects the record associated with the AWS Region that gives the lowest latency only among the records that actually exist for the name; if no record was created for ap-southeast-1, that Region can never be selected no matter how much lower its latency would be. There is no minimum record count requirement (A), and latency routing is based on measured network latency data, not creation order (C).

stem: An application requires the true client source IP address to be visible at the TCP layer without parsing HTTP headers, needs to preserve extremely low latency, and must pass through TLS untouched end to end to the backend. Which load balancer type should be used, and why is the alternative unsuitable?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer, because it adds an X-Forwarded-For header with the client IP
Network Load Balancer, because it operates at Layer 4 and preserves the original client source IP natively without needing a header or proxy protocol
Application Load Balancer with proxy protocol v2 enabled, because ALB supports proxy protocol natively
Network Load Balancer, because it terminates TLS and re-encrypts to the backend using ACM certificates

explanation: NLB operates at the connection level (Layer 4) and by default preserves the client's source IP address in the packet itself, and it can pass TLS through untouched, meeting all three requirements natively. ALB (A, C) terminates TCP/TLS at Layer 7 and communicates client IP via the X-Forwarded-For header rather than preserving it in the packet, and ALB does not support proxy protocol the way NLB does.

stem: A security team wants to insert third-party virtual firewall appliances transparently in front of multiple VPCs to inspect all traffic, with the appliance fleet scaling automatically based on load, using GENEVE encapsulation to preserve the original packet for inspection. Which load balancing service is purpose-built for this?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer with a Lambda target
Gateway Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer with UDP listeners
Classic Load Balancer with an auto scaling group of appliances

explanation: Gateway Load Balancer is specifically designed for deploying, scaling, and managing third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls and intrusion detection systems, using the GENEVE protocol on port 6081 to encapsulate traffic for transparent inspection while distributing load across the appliance fleet. Neither ALB (A) nor plain NLB (C) provide the GENEVE-based transparent bump-in-the-wire insertion model GWLB offers.

stem: A team is deciding whether to enable cross-zone load balancing on a Network Load Balancer that currently has an uneven number of registered targets per Availability Zone, causing some targets to receive disproportionately more traffic. What is the tradeoff of enabling cross-zone load balancing on this NLB?

choices.text: Enabling it evens out the distribution of requests across all targets regardless of AZ, but traffic that crosses an AZ boundary incurs standard cross-AZ data transfer charges
Enabling it is free and has no effect on traffic distribution, only on health check frequency
NLB cross-zone load balancing cannot be changed after the load balancer is created
Enabling it disables preservation of the client source IP address

explanation: Unlike ALB (which always cross-zone load balances at no extra charge), NLB cross-zone load balancing is off by default and can be enabled per load balancer or target group; enabling it distributes requests evenly across all registered targets in all enabled AZs but data transferred across an AZ boundary is billed as cross-AZ data transfer. It can be changed after creation (C is false) and has no effect on source IP preservation (D is false).

stem: An application team changed a target group's health check path from /status to /health as part of a routine cleanup, but the application only implements a health endpoint at /status. Shortly after, all targets in the target group are marked unhealthy and the ALB begins returning 503 errors to clients. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Increase the healthy threshold count so targets are marked healthy faster
Revert the health check path to /health check the deregistration delay setting instead
Update the target group's health check path back to /status, or implement a /health endpoint on the application that returns a successful response
Increase the health check timeout to 300 seconds

explanation: The targets are failing health checks because the configured health check path (/health) does not exist on the application, which only serves /status; the fix is to align the health check path configuration with an actual working endpoint on the targets. Increasing thresholds, timeouts, or adjusting deregistration delay (A, B, D) does not address a health check hitting a nonexistent path that returns a non-2xx/3xx response.

stem: An Application Load Balancer needs to keep a given user's requests routed to the same target for the duration of their shopping session, using a cookie that the ALB itself generates and manages rather than one issued by the application. Which sticky session mechanism does this describe?

choices.text: Application-based cookie stickiness using the AWSALBAPP cookie
Duration-based cookie stickiness using the AWSALB cookie generated by the load balancer
Source IP-based stickiness
Sticky sessions are only available on Network Load Balancer, not ALB

explanation: Duration-based stickiness uses a load-balancer-generated cookie named AWSALB (or AWSALBCORS for CORS-enabled requests) to bind a client's requests to a specific target for a configurable duration, without any application involvement. Application-based stickiness (A) instead relies on a cookie that the application itself generates and the ALB then wraps in AWSALBAPP, which is a different mechanism than described.

stem: During a rolling deployment behind an ALB, instances are deregistered from the target group as new instances come online. Users report dropped connections and failed in-flight requests at the moment old instances are deregistered, even though the deployment tooling waits for new targets to become healthy first. What setting should be adjusted to fix this?

choices.text: Increase the target group's deregistration delay (connection draining) so in-flight requests can complete before the target is fully removed
Decrease the health check interval on the target group
Enable cross-zone load balancing on the target group
Switch from an Application Load Balancer to a Network Load Balancer

explanation: The deregistration delay (connection draining) setting controls how long the load balancer waits before completing the deregistration of a target, continuing to send it existing in-flight requests but no new ones; if this value is too low, active requests are cut off. Health check interval (B) and cross-zone load balancing (C) do not control in-flight request completion during deregistration.

stem: A partner integration requires the customer to allow-list a small, fixed set of IP addresses per Availability Zone for an internet-facing load balancer, and the load balancer must support this without additional infrastructure such as Global Accelerator. Which load balancer type supports this requirement natively?

choices.text: Application Load Balancer, which supports a fixed Elastic IP per AZ by default
Network Load Balancer, which supports one static IP address (or Elastic IP) per subnet/AZ
Classic Load Balancer, which uses a single global static IP
Gateway Load Balancer, which exposes a static IP for internet-facing traffic

explanation: Network Load Balancer natively provides one static IP address per enabled AZ (or lets you assign your own Elastic IP), making it straightforward to give partners a fixed, small set of IPs to allow-list. ALB (A) uses DNS-resolved IP addresses that can change over time and does not offer static IPs without pairing with Global Accelerator, and GWLB (D) is not designed for internet-facing static IP exposure to end clients.

stem: A company runs api.example.com and www.example.com behind the same Application Load Balancer and needs requests routed to different target groups purely based on the requested domain name in the request, independent of the URL path. Which ALB routing capability should they configure?

choices.text: Path-based routing rules matching on /api/* and /www/*
Host-based routing rules matching on the Host header for api.example.com and www.example.com
Query string-based routing rules
Source IP-based routing rules

explanation: Host-based routing lets an ALB listener rule route requests to different target groups based on the Host header (domain name) in the request, which is exactly what distinguishing api.example.com from www.example.com requires. Path-based routing (A) instead matches on the URL path, which is a different dimension not tied to the domain name requested.

stem: A centralized inspection architecture routes VPC traffic through Gateway Load Balancer endpoints to a fleet of stateful firewall appliances behind a Gateway Load Balancer. Engineers observe that some flows are inspected correctly, but for other flows the return traffic takes a different path through a different Availability Zone than the outbound leg, causing the stateful firewall to drop the traffic as unrecognized. What should be enabled to fix this?

choices.text: Cross-zone load balancing on the Gateway Load Balancer
Appliance mode on the Gateway Load Balancer endpoint, so all traffic for a given flow is consistently routed to the same target/AZ
Sticky sessions on the Gateway Load Balancer target group using source IP affinity
A dedicated NAT gateway per Availability Zone in the inspection VPC

explanation: Appliance mode on a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint ensures that all traffic for a given flow, in both directions, is consistently routed to the same GWLB target and stays within the same Availability Zone, which resolves asymmetric routing issues that break stateful inspection. Cross-zone load balancing (A) affects distribution across GWLB targets generally but does not guarantee flow-level symmetry the way appliance mode does.

stem: A team is choosing between terminating TLS at an Application Load Balancer versus passing TLS through end to end on a Network Load Balancer. Terminating at the ALB allows centralized certificate management with ACM and enables host- and path-based routing, but the team is concerned about compliance requirements for true end-to-end encryption. What is the correct tradeoff assessment?

choices.text: NLB TLS passthrough preserves true end-to-end encryption to the backend but sacrifices Layer 7 routing features and centralizes nothing at the load balancer; ALB termination enables centralized cert management and L7 routing but breaks true end-to-end encryption unless the ALB also re-encrypts to the backend
There is no difference; both ALB and NLB always re-encrypt traffic to the backend using ACM-issued certificates
NLB cannot handle TLS traffic at all, so ALB termination is the only option for HTTPS workloads
ALB termination always preserves end-to-end encryption because ACM certificates are used on both legs by default

explanation: With TLS passthrough on an NLB, the load balancer forwards encrypted TCP traffic untouched to the backend, preserving genuine end-to-end encryption but giving up any Layer 7 inspection or routing since the LB never sees plaintext; ALB termination decrypts at the load balancer for routing and centralized certificate management, which means the connection to the backend is a separate TLS session (or plaintext) unless explicitly re-encrypted. NLB fully supports TLS via a TLS listener (C is false).

stem: A security team needs VPC Flow Logs delivered to a third-party SIEM in near real time via a streaming pipeline, while a separate compliance team needs the same flow log data retained cheaply for seven years and queried occasionally with Amazon Athena. Which two flow log destinations should be configured to meet both needs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose, streaming to the third-party SIEM for near real-time delivery
Amazon S3, for low-cost long-term retention and ad hoc querying with Athena
AWS CloudTrail, for both real-time streaming and long-term retention
Amazon CloudWatch Logs only, for both requirements
AWS Config, for long-term retention and Athena querying

explanation: VPC Flow Logs can be delivered directly to Kinesis Data Firehose for near real-time streaming to third-party destinations, and separately to Amazon S3 for cost-effective long-term storage that Athena can query directly. CloudTrail (C) and AWS Config (E) record API activity and configuration changes respectively, not network flow data, so neither is a valid flow log destination.

stem: A company operates dozens of VPCs across multiple accounts and wants centralized, queryable logs of every DNS query made by resources within those VPCs, including the query name, response, and the instance that issued it, for security investigations. Which capability should they configure?

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs with the additional DNS fields enabled
Route 53 Resolver query logging, with a query logging configuration associated to the VPCs (including shared cross-account) and delivered to a centralized CloudWatch Logs group or S3 bucket
AWS CloudTrail data events for Route 53
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall alert logs only

explanation: Route 53 Resolver query logging captures details of DNS queries made by resources within associated VPCs, including query name, type, and response, and a single query logging configuration can be associated with multiple VPCs, including ones shared cross-account, with logs delivered centrally to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Kinesis Data Firehose. VPC Flow Logs (A) record IP traffic metadata, not DNS query content.

stem: A global enterprise has dozens of Transit Gateways, Direct Connect connections, and Site-to-Site VPN connections spread across multiple Regions and accounts, along with on-premises SD-WAN devices. Leadership wants a single visual representation of the entire network topology and its real-time operational status. Which service should be used to build this?

choices.text: AWS Transit Gateway Network Manager, using a global network resource to register and visualize transit gateways, on-premises devices, links, and sites
Amazon CloudWatch dashboards built manually per Region
AWS Config aggregator with a custom conformance pack
VPC Reachability Analyzer run against each Transit Gateway individually

explanation: Transit Gateway Network Manager lets you create a global network object that registers Transit Gateways across Regions and accounts, along with on-premises sites, links, and devices (including third-party SD-WAN), providing a unified topology view and operational metrics in one console. Reachability Analyzer (D) checks specific path reachability between two resources rather than providing a holistic topology view.

stem: A network team wants to continuously measure packet loss and latency on the path between their AWS VPCs and an on-premises data center reached over Direct Connect, without deploying any monitoring agent or software on the on-premises servers themselves. Which capability fits this requirement?

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs analyzed with Amazon Athena
Amazon CloudWatch Network Monitor, which uses probes deployed in the VPC to actively measure performance to specified on-premises destination IP addresses without requiring on-premises agents
AWS Network Manager Route Analyzer
Direct Connect connection-level CloudWatch metrics only

explanation: Amazon CloudWatch Network Monitor creates monitors that use lightweight probes running from specified VPC subnets to continuously test latency and packet loss to defined on-premises IP addresses, without needing any agent installed on the on-premises side. Flow Logs (A) provide traffic metadata, not active latency/loss measurement, and Route Analyzer (C) checks routing configuration and reachability rather than continuous performance metrics.

stem: A team is enabling VPC Flow Logs and debating whether to configure them at the VPC level, subnet level, or individual network interface (ENI) level for a VPC that will have many auto-scaled instances created and terminated over time. Which approach requires the least ongoing configuration effort while still capturing all traffic?

choices.text: ENI level, configuring a new flow log for each instance as it launches
VPC level, which automatically covers all subnets and all current and future ENIs within the VPC
Subnet level only for the subnets that exist today
Flow logs must always be configured per ENI; there is no VPC or subnet level option

explanation: Enabling flow logs at the VPC level automatically applies to every subnet and every network interface within that VPC, including ones created later by auto scaling, with no per-instance configuration needed. ENI-level (A) or subnet-level-only (C) configuration would require ongoing manual effort to keep up with newly launched instances or subnets.

stem: Traffic between two VPC attachments on a Transit Gateway is intermittently failing, and the network team suspects packets are being dropped at the Transit Gateway itself rather than within either VPC. Which logging capability should be enabled to directly observe accepted and rejected traffic at the Transit Gateway level?

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs on both VPCs' subnets, since they capture Transit Gateway traffic natively
Transit Gateway Flow Logs, which capture traffic accepted or rejected by the Transit Gateway itself, separate from VPC Flow Logs
AWS CloudTrail management events for the Transit Gateway
Route 53 Resolver query logging on the Transit Gateway attachments

explanation: Transit Gateway Flow Logs are a distinct feature from VPC Flow Logs and capture information about the IP traffic going through the Transit Gateway itself, including whether it was accepted or rejected at the TGW routing layer, which is exactly what is needed to isolate a TGW-level drop from a VPC-level issue. Standard VPC Flow Logs (A) only reflect traffic at the ENI/subnet/VPC boundary, not the TGW's internal routing decisions.

stem: A network engineer suspects that traffic is not reaching its intended destination because of a missing or blackholed route somewhere along a multi-hop path through a Transit Gateway with several route tables. Rather than manually inspecting every route table, which tool can trace the expected path and identify the specific configuration issue?

choices.text: AWS Network Manager Route Analyzer
VPC Reachability Analyzer only, since it is the sole tool that understands Transit Gateway route tables
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries against VPC Flow Logs
AWS Trusted Advisor network reachability checks

explanation: Network Manager's Route Analyzer traces the path between a specified source and destination across Transit Gateway attachments and route tables, identifying issues such as blackhole routes, missing routes, or asymmetric paths. While VPC Reachability Analyzer (B) can also trace paths, Route Analyzer is the Network Manager tool purpose-built for multi-account, multi-Region Transit Gateway route table analysis referenced here.

stem: A platform team wants to proactively detect when traffic through a specific Transit Gateway VPC attachment is approaching its per-attachment bandwidth limit before applications experience throttling or packet loss. Which CloudWatch metrics should they monitor and alarm on?

choices.text: BytesIn, BytesOut, and PacketDropCount metrics published by Transit Gateway per attachment
CPUUtilization of the EC2 instances behind the attachment
Route 53 health check status for the attachment
S3 request metrics for the VPC's flow log destination bucket

explanation: Transit Gateway publishes per-attachment CloudWatch metrics including BytesIn, BytesOut, PacketsIn, PacketsOut, and PacketDropCount, which can be monitored and alarmed on to detect an attachment approaching its bandwidth ceiling (each VPC attachment has a per-attachment burst limit) before drops occur. Instance CPU (B) or Route 53 health checks (C) do not reflect Transit Gateway attachment-level throughput.

stem: A large AWS Organization wants VPC Flow Logs from over 100 member accounts consolidated into a single central security account for analysis, without requiring each account team to manually configure cross-account permissions individually. What is an efficient way to achieve this centrally?

choices.text: Have each of the 100 accounts manually create an IAM role trust policy to the security account and email the ARNs to the central team

Enable flow log delivery to a centralized Amazon S3 bucket in the security account with a bucket policy allowing delivery from the organization, deployed consistently via infrastructure-as-code or an AWS Organizations service, so member accounts only need to reference the central bucket as the log destination
Copy each account's flow logs manually on a weekly schedule using the AWS CLI
Flow logs cannot be delivered cross-account; each account must retain and analyze its own logs separately

explanation: VPC Flow Logs can be delivered directly to a centralized S3 bucket owned by another account, provided the bucket policy grants the necessary delivery permissions; combined with AWS Organizations and infrastructure-as-code (or delegated administration) to apply this consistently, flow logs from many member accounts can be consolidated into one central account without per-account manual coordination. Cross-account delivery is fully supported (D is false).

stem: A company has two 10 Gbps dedicated Direct Connect connections terminating on the same AWS Direct Connect device and wants to combine them into a single logical connection for both increased aggregate bandwidth and resiliency against a single physical connection failure. What should they configure, and what constraint must be satisfied?

choices.text: A Link Aggregation Group (LAG), which requires all member connections to have the same bandwidth and terminate at the same AWS Direct Connect endpoint
A Direct Connect Gateway, which automatically aggregates bandwidth across any two connections in the same account
A Transit Gateway Connect attachment, which merges multiple physical connections into one logical GRE tunnel
Two separate private VIFs advertising the same prefix with equal BGP weights

explanation: A LAG combines multiple Direct Connect connections into a single logical connection, treated as one for bandwidth and redundancy purposes, but all member connections must have the same bandwidth and terminate at the same AWS Direct Connect device/endpoint. A Direct Connect Gateway (B) is used to connect DX to multiple VPCs/VIFs, not to aggregate physical connection bandwidth.

stem: A company has a single Direct Connect connection and needs it to provide connectivity to VPCs located in five different AWS Regions across two accounts, using a single BGP session rather than one private VIF per VPC. Which Direct Connect construct is required?

choices.text: Five private VIFs, one per Region, sharing the same BGP session
A Direct Connect Gateway associated with a Transit VIF and Transit Gateways (or Direct Connect Gateway VPC associations) in each Region
A hosted VIF for each additional Region beyond the first
AWS Direct Connect SiteLink connecting each Region's VPC directly

explanation: A Direct Connect Gateway paired with a Transit VIF allows a single Direct Connect connection and BGP session to reach Transit Gateways (and therefore many VPCs) across multiple Regions and accounts, since Direct Connect Gateway itself is a global resource; a private VIF (A, C), by contrast, can only be associated with a single VGW/VPC. SiteLink (D) provides connectivity between Direct Connect locations, not VPC association.

stem: An on-premises network advertises the same prefix to AWS over two Direct Connect private VIFs terminating at different AWS Direct Connect locations. The network team wants AWS to prefer sending return traffic over Connection A whenever it is available, only using Connection B if A is down. Which BGP technique achieves this preference for AWS-to-on-premises traffic?

choices.text: Prepend the on-premises AS number additional times on the BGP advertisement sent over Connection B, making its AS path longer and therefore less preferred by AWS
Set a higher MED value on Connection A's advertisement
Configure a static route on the AWS side pointing only to Connection A
Increase the BGP keepalive interval on Connection B

explanation: AS path prepending on the less-preferred path (Connection B) makes its advertised route appear to traverse more autonomous systems, and since BGP prefers shorter AS paths all else being equal, AWS will prefer the shorter, non-prepended path over Connection A for return traffic. A higher MED (B) on Connection A would need to be lower, not higher, to be preferred, and MED is only considered after AS path length in the standard decision process.

stem: A company relies on a single Direct Connect connection for production traffic and wants a Site-to-Site VPN as an automatic backup path that only carries traffic when Direct Connect is unavailable, using dynamic BGP routing on both paths to the same VPC. How should this be configured so Direct Connect is preferred whenever healthy?

choices.text: Configure BGP on both the Direct Connect private VIF and the VPN connection to the same VGW/Transit Gateway, and apply AS path prepending on the VPN-advertised routes so the VPN path is naturally deprioritized while healthy Direct Connect routes are shorter and preferred
Configure only static routes on the VPN, since BGP is not supported over Site-to-Site VPN
Disable the VPN connection entirely and manually enable it only during a Direct Connect outage
Set the VPN connection's BGP ASN to match the Direct Connect ASN exactly so AWS treats them as a single path

explanation: When both Direct Connect and VPN advertise routes via BGP to the same gateway, AWS Direct Connect connections are preferred by default over an equivalent BGP-advertised VPN path when both are healthy; adding AS path prepending on the VPN side reinforces that preference so failover only occurs when Direct Connect's BGP session actually goes down. BGP is fully supported over Site-to-Site VPN (B is false), and manually toggling the VPN (C) defeats the purpose of automatic failover.

stem: A multinational company has Direct Connect connections established at Direct Connect locations in two different countries and wants to send traffic directly between those two on-premises sites through the AWS Direct Connect network backbone, without that traffic being routed through a VPC or an AWS Region. Which Direct Connect feature enables this?

choices.text: AWS Direct Connect SiteLink
A Direct Connect Gateway with a private VIF in each Region
Transit Gateway inter-Region peering
AWS Global Accelerator with custom routing

explanation: SiteLink is a Direct Connect feature that allows traffic to flow directly between any two Direct Connect locations connected through a shared Direct Connect Gateway, bypassing the need to route through a VPC or a specific AWS Region, reducing latency for site-to-site traffic. A standard Direct Connect Gateway setup with private VIFs (B) still routes through VPCs/VGWs in a Region rather than directly between Direct Connect locations.

stem: A regulated customer requires Layer 2 encryption on their Direct Connect connections to protect data in transit at line rate without the overhead of IPsec. Which Direct Connect feature should they enable, and what connection type is it supported on?

choices.text: MACsec, supported on dedicated Direct Connect connections at eligible speeds such as 10 Gbps and 100 Gbps
IPsec over Direct Connect, supported on all hosted connections regardless of speed
TLS 1.3 termination at the Direct Connect router
MACsec, supported only on hosted connections shared through a Direct Connect Partner

explanation: MACsec (Media Access Control Security) provides native Layer 2, line-rate encryption on eligible AWS Direct Connect dedicated connections at qualifying speeds (such as 10 Gbps and 100 Gbps), avoiding the throughput overhead associated with IPsec tunneling. MACsec is not available on hosted connections (D is false), and Direct Connect itself does not offer IPsec or TLS termination as a connection feature in this way.

stem: A company uses SD-WAN appliances on-premises and wants to integrate them with a Transit Gateway using dynamic BGP routing over a GRE-based tunnel that supports higher throughput per tunnel than a standard Site-to-Site VPN attachment. Which Transit Gateway feature should they use?

choices.text: Transit Gateway Connect attachment, using GRE tunnels with BGP for dynamic routing and higher per-attachment bandwidth than a VPN attachment
A standard Site-to-Site VPN attachment with two tunnels for higher bandwidth
A VPC peering connection between the SD-WAN VPC and the Transit Gateway VPC
A Direct Connect Transit VIF, which is required for any SD-WAN integration

explanation: Transit Gateway Connect attachments use GRE tunnels (over an existing VPC or Direct Connect attachment) combined with BGP to provide dynamic routing to SD-WAN appliances, and each Connect attachment supports substantially higher bandwidth per tunnel than a standard IPsec VPN attachment. A standard VPN attachment (B) is limited to roughly 1.25 Gbps per tunnel and is not GRE-based.

stem: A hybrid network experiences intermittent BGP session flaps between an on-premises router and AWS over a Direct Connect connection, and each flap causes a 60-90 second outage while BGP hold timers expire before failover to a backup path completes. What should be implemented to detect the failure and trigger failover much faster?

choices.text: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD), which detects link failures in milliseconds and can be configured alongside BGP on the Direct Connect connection
Increase the BGP hold timer to 180 seconds to reduce false flaps
Switch from BGP to static routing to eliminate hold timers entirely
Enable ECMP across the Direct Connect connection

explanation: BFD provides sub-second failure detection independent of the BGP hold timer, and AWS Direct Connect supports BFD alongside BGP so that a failed path is detected and failover initiated far faster than waiting for the default 90-second BGP hold timer to expire. Increasing the hold timer (B) would make detection slower, not faster, and static routing (C) removes the dynamic failover capability altogether.

stem: A company needs a new Direct Connect connection quickly and does not want to manage physical cross-connects or a dedicated port at an AWS Direct Connect location, and is fine with a Direct Connect Partner provisioning a sub-1-Gbps connection on shared infrastructure. Which connection type should they order, and what capability do they give up compared to the alternative?

choices.text: A hosted connection through an AWS Direct Connect Partner; they give up the ability to create a LAG or use MACsec, both of which require a dedicated connection
A dedicated connection ordered directly from AWS; they give up the ability to use BGP
A hosted connection; there is no functional difference from a dedicated connection at any speed
A dedicated connection; hosted connections are being deprecated by AWS

explanation: Hosted connections are provisioned by an AWS Direct Connect Partner on their shared infrastructure, are available at a range of sub-1-Gbps to higher speeds and are quicker to provision without managing a dedicated port, but they cannot be combined into a LAG and do not support MACsec, both of which require a dedicated connection ordered directly from AWS. BGP is supported on both connection types (B is false).

stem: A company relies on Direct Connect with jumbo frames (9001 MTU) enabled end to end for a data replication workload that depends on high throughput. As a resiliency improvement, they add a Site-to-Site VPN as a BGP-advertised backup path to the same Transit Gateway. During a scheduled Direct Connect maintenance window, traffic fails over to the VPN and replication throughput drops sharply with intermittent errors related to oversized packets. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Site-to-Site VPN tunnels do not support jumbo frames the way Direct Connect does, so packets sized for a 9001 MTU path are being dropped or fragmented once traffic shifts to the VPN
BGP does not support failover between Direct Connect and VPN, so traffic is being black-holed rather than actually using the VPN
Transit Gateway VPN attachments do not support BGP, forcing a switch to static routing that drops large packets
The VPN connection must be re-established manually after every Direct Connect maintenance event, so no traffic was flowing at all

explanation: AWS Site-to-Site VPN tunnels have a lower effective MTU than Direct Connect (Direct Connect supports jumbo frames up to 9001 MTU, while VPN traffic is limited to a smaller payload due to IPsec/GRE overhead), so applications sending jumbo-sized packets over Direct Connect will experience fragmentation or drops if they are not adjusted when failing over to VPN. BGP failover between DX and VPN attachments to the same Transit Gateway is a standard supported pattern (B and C are false).

stem: A company has 20 VPCs across several accounts that all need full any-to-any IP connectivity, and the number of VPCs is expected to keep growing. Using VPC peering, this would require up to 190 individual peering connections and per-VPC route table entries for every other VPC. What architecture significantly simplifies this as the VPC count grows?

choices.text: A hub-and-spoke design using a Transit Gateway, where each VPC has a single attachment to the Transit Gateway and routing is centralized in Transit Gateway route tables
A full mesh of VPC peering connections, since peering has no limit on the number of connections per VPC
A single shared VPC using VPC sharing (RAM) for all 20 workloads instead of separate VPCs
Multiple Direct Connect Gateways, one per VPC, connected to a common Direct Connect connection

explanation: Transit Gateway lets each VPC maintain just one attachment regardless of how many other VPCs it needs to reach, with routing centralized and managed through Transit Gateway route tables, scaling far more simply than the roughly n(n-1)/2 peering connections a full mesh would require as VPCs are added. VPC peering (B) does have practical account and per-VPC connection limits and does not support transitive routing.

stem: A network architect is comparing VPC Peering and Transit Gateway for connecting a growing number of VPCs. Which two statements correctly describe disadvantages of VPC Peering relative to Transit Gateway in this context? (Select TWO)

choices.text: VPC Peering connections are not transitive, so a peered VPC cannot route through an intermediary VPC to reach a third VPC it is not directly peered with
Each VPC can only maintain a limited number of active peering connections, requiring careful management as the number of VPCs grows
VPC Peering charges an hourly attachment fee per connection, unlike Transit Gateway
VPC Peering cannot be used across different AWS accounts
VPC Peering does not support communication between resources at all, only DNS resolution

explanation: VPC Peering connections are strictly non-transitive, meaning connectivity must be direct between each pair of VPCs, and each VPC has a practical limit on the number of peering connections it can maintain, both of which become operationally harder to manage as the VPC count grows compared to Transit Gateway's centralized hub model. VPC Peering has no hourly connection charge (C is false, unlike Transit Gateway attachments) and does support cross-account peering (D is false).

stem: A company wants all outbound internet traffic from dozens of spoke VPCs to egress through a single centralized set of NAT gateways in a shared services VPC, rather than deploying NAT gateways in every spoke VPC, in order to reduce cost and centralize egress monitoring. How should this be architected using Transit Gateway?

choices.text: Attach the shared services VPC (containing the NAT gateways) and all spoke VPCs to a Transit Gateway; spoke VPC route tables send 0.0.0.0/0 to the Transit Gateway, and the Transit Gateway route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the shared services VPC attachment
Create a NAT gateway in every spoke VPC and use Transit Gateway only for east-west traffic between spokes
Use VPC endpoints for all internet-bound traffic instead of NAT gateways
Peer every spoke VPC directly with the shared services VPC and route 0.0.0.0/0 over each peering connection

explanation: Centralized egress works by attaching a shared services VPC containing the NAT gateway(s) to the Transit Gateway alongside all spoke VPCs; each spoke sends its default route to the Transit Gateway, and the Transit Gateway route table forwards default-route traffic to the shared services VPC attachment, consolidating NAT infrastructure and cost. Deploying NAT gateways per spoke VPC (B) is exactly the cost and management overhead this design avoids.

stem: A company must ensure that a set of VPCs handling PCI-regulated workloads can never establish direct network connectivity to a set of general-purpose VPCs, even though both sets are attached to the same Transit Gateway and occasionally need to reach a shared services VPC. How should Transit Gateway route tables be designed?

choices.text: Create separate Transit Gateway route tables for the PCI VPCs and the general-purpose VPCs, associate each attachment with only its respective route table, and selectively propagate routes so only the shared services VPC's routes appear in both, while the PCI and general-purpose route tables never propagate routes to each other
Use a single Transit Gateway route table for all attachments and rely on security groups alone to block traffic between PCI and general-purpose VPCs
Attach the PCI VPCs to a completely separate Transit Gateway and manually copy security group rules between the two Transit Gateways
Disable route propagation entirely on the Transit Gateway and only use VPC-level network ACLs for segmentation

explanation: Transit Gateway supports multiple route tables, and by associating each attachment with a specific route table and controlling which routes are propagated into each table, you can enforce that PCI VPCs and general-purpose VPCs only see routes to shared services (not to each other), achieving network-layer segmentation independent of security groups. Relying solely on security groups (B) leaves an underlying routed path available and does not achieve true network segmentation at the routing layer.

stem: VPC A and VPC B are both attached to the same Transit Gateway, but instances in VPC A cannot reach instances in VPC B despite the Transit Gateway route table showing a propagated route for VPC B's CIDR. What else must be verified to fully troubleshoot this?

choices.text: That VPC A's subnet route table has a route for VPC B's CIDR pointing at the Transit Gateway attachment, since the Transit Gateway route table alone does not affect routing within the VPC's own subnets
That the Transit Gateway route table is using static routes instead of propagation, since propagation never actually installs a usable route
That both VPCs are in the same Availability Zone
That the Transit Gateway has multicast support enabled

explanation: Connectivity through a Transit Gateway requires routes at multiple layers: the VPC subnet route tables must have a route for the remote CIDR pointing at the local Transit Gateway attachment (this is separate from and in addition to the Transit Gateway's own route table), and the Transit Gateway route table associated with the sending attachment must have a route (static or propagated) to the destination. Propagated routes are fully functional routes (B is false), and AZ alignment (C) is not a Transit Gateway routing requirement.

stem: A company deploys a centralized inspection VPC with a Gateway Load Balancer and stateful firewall appliances to inspect east-west traffic between spoke VPCs, all connected through a Transit Gateway. Testing reveals that some flows between two spoke VPCs are being dropped by the firewall because outbound and return traffic for the same flow are inspected by different firewall appliance instances in different Availability Zones. What should be enabled to fix this for VPC-to-VPC (east-west) inspection through Transit Gateway?

choices.text: Appliance mode on the Transit Gateway VPC attachment connecting to the inspection VPC, ensuring flow symmetry across Availability Zones
Multicast support on the Transit Gateway
Cross-zone load balancing on the Transit Gateway itself
A second Transit Gateway dedicated only to return traffic

explanation: For centralized east-west inspection architectures, enabling appliance mode on the Transit Gateway attachment to the inspection VPC ensures that traffic for a given flow, in both directions, is consistently sent to the same Availability Zone (and therefore the same appliance instance), preventing asymmetric inspection failures. Transit Gateway itself has no 'cross-zone load balancing' setting (C); that concept applies to the Gateway Load Balancer, not the Transit Gateway attachment directly.

stem: Two Transit Gateways in different Regions, each with their own set of attached VPCs, need to exchange routes so that VPCs attached to one can reach VPCs attached to the other, without traffic traversing the public internet. Which approach should be used, and what routing limitation applies?

choices.text: A Transit Gateway peering attachment between the two Transit Gateways; routes across the peering attachment must be added as static routes, since dynamic route propagation is not supported over a Transit Gateway peering attachment
A Transit Gateway peering attachment; routes are automatically propagated across the peering attachment just like any VPC attachment
VPC peering directly between VPCs in the two Regions instead of Transit Gateway peering
AWS PrivateLink between the two Transit Gateways

explanation: Transit Gateway peering attachments connect Transit Gateways across Regions (or accounts) privately over the AWS backbone, but route propagation is not supported across a peering attachment, so static routes must be added in each Transit Gateway's route table pointing at the peering attachment for the remote CIDRs. Automatic propagation (B) does not apply to peering attachments, and PrivateLink (D) is not used to connect two Transit Gateways.

stem: A media processing company needs to send the same video stream from a single source instance to multiple receiver instances across several VPCs attached to the same Transit Gateway, using IP multicast rather than replicating unicast streams to each receiver individually. Which Transit Gateway feature supports this?

choices.text: Transit Gateway Connect attachments
Transit Gateway multicast domains, which allow sources and receivers using IGMPv2 (or static group membership) across attached VPCs to participate in multicast groups
Transit Gateway peering attachments with broadcast mode enabled
VPC Flow Logs configured with a multicast filter

explanation: Transit Gateway supports multicast domains, allowing EC2 instances in different attached VPCs to act as multicast sources and receivers within the same multicast group, using IGMPv2 for dynamic group membership or statically configured members. Connect attachments (A) are used for SD-WAN/GRE integration and are unrelated to multicast distribution.

stem: A central network team owns and operates a Transit Gateway in a dedicated networking account and needs to make it available so that 30 other accounts in the AWS Organization can create their own VPC attachments to it, without the central team creating and managing each attachment on behalf of every other account. What should they do?

choices.text: Share the Transit Gateway with the other accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), after which each account can create its own VPC attachment to the shared Transit Gateway
Manually create a VPC attachment in the central account for every other account's VPC by assuming a role into each account
Copy the Transit Gateway configuration into each of the 30 accounts using AWS CloudFormation StackSets
Enable AWS Organizations delegated administrator for Transit Gateway, which automatically attaches all member account VPCs

explanation: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) lets the owning account share a Transit Gateway with other accounts (or the whole Organization), after which those accounts can create their own VPC attachments to the shared Transit Gateway using their own VPC resources, without the central team having to manage attachments on their behalf. Manually assuming roles into every account (B) works but defeats the purpose of decentralized self-service attachment creation that RAM provides.

stem: A network engineer is provisioning a new AWS Direct Connect connection at a MACsec-capable location and wants to eventually encrypt traffic on the link using MACsec. Which statement about MACsec on Direct Connect is correct?

choices.text: MACsec can be enabled on hosted connections created by an AWS Direct Connect Partner
MACsec requires a dedicated connection with a port speed of 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps at a MACsec-capable device
MACsec encrypts traffic between the customer router and the Direct Connect location using IPsec
MACsec is enabled automatically on all Direct Connect LAGs without additional configuration

explanation: MACsec is supported only on dedicated Direct Connect connections (not hosted connections) at 10 Gbps and 100 Gbps ports on MACsec-capable devices, and it operates at Layer 2 (802.1AE), not IPsec. It must be explicitly configured with a CKN/CAK pair rather than enabled automatically.

stem: A company has a 100 Gbps Direct Connect LAG composed of two 100 Gbps dedicated connections at a MACsec-capable location and wants to enable MACsec encryption across the LAG. Which requirement must be satisfied?

choices.text: Only one of the two member connections needs a CKN/CAK key pair, and AWS replicates it to the other member
Each member connection in the LAG must have its own independent MACsec security association (CKN/CAK) configured
MACsec can only be enabled after all member connections are deleted and recreated as a hosted connection
LAG member connections automatically share a single MACsec session negotiated at the LAG level

explanation: MACsec is configured per physical connection, so each LAG member must have its own independently established CKN/CAK association for encryption to take effect on that member's traffic. AWS does not replicate keys across members or negotiate one shared session at the LAG level.

stem: After enabling MACsec "must secure" mode on one member connection of a two-member Direct Connect LAG, traffic across that member drops to zero while the other member continues to pass traffic normally, and BGP is up on both connections. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The LAG minimum links threshold was not met
The customer router's MACsec key (CKN/CAK) does not match the AWS-side key for that connection, so the secure channel never establishes and must-secure mode blocks all unencrypted traffic
The other LAG member is drawing all traffic due to BGP local preference
MACsec cannot be enabled independently per member, so this configuration is not possible

explanation: In must-secure mode, if MACsec key negotiation fails due to mismatched CKN/CAK values, the connection blocks all unencrypted traffic on that link, effectively taking it down for data traffic. MACsec is in fact configured per LAG member (ruling out D), and neither the LAG threshold nor local preference explains a hard drop tied specifically to enabling must-secure mode.

stem: A company has two Direct Connect connections at two different Direct Connect locations, both advertising the same on-premises prefix to AWS via BGP. They want AWS-to-on-premises traffic to prefer Connection A and use Connection B only as backup. Which action on the on-premises routers achieves this using AS path manipulation?

choices.text: Prepend the AS path on the routes advertised from on-premises over Connection B so the path appears longer to AWS
Increase the BGP local preference on the routes received from Connection B
Set a lower MED on the routes advertised over Connection A
Prepend the AS path on routes advertised from AWS over Connection A

explanation: To influence traffic flowing from AWS toward on-premises, the customer prepends its own AS number on routes advertised over the less-preferred path, making that path look longer so AWS prefers Connection A. Local preference is set by the receiving AS on its own routers and isn't something the customer configures on AWS's side, and MED is only a tie-breaker among paths from the same neighboring AS.

stem: An enterprise has two Direct Connect private VIFs terminating in the same AWS Region from two different on-premises routers, both advertising the same on-premises prefix. They want AWS to consistently prefer routes from VIF A over VIF B without changing AS path length. Which approach is correct per AWS Direct Connect's supported BGP mechanisms?

choices.text: Tag the routes advertised over VIF B with the AWS-defined low-preference BGP community so AWS assigns them a lower local preference than the routes on VIF A
Configure a static route on the AWS side with a higher administrative distance for VIF B
Set a higher MED value on routes advertised over VIF A, since AWS Direct Connect always prefers the highest MED
Open an AWS Support case to have AWS Support manually adjust BGP local preference for the customer's ASN

explanation: AWS Direct Connect recognizes specific BGP community tags customers can attach to advertised routes to signal desired local preference for reaching the same Region over multiple connections, letting AWS set local preference internally without altering AS path length. Static routes and manual AWS Support intervention are not the supported mechanism, and BGP prefers lower, not higher, MED values.

stem: An enterprise advertises the same on-premises prefix over two separate Direct Connect private VIFs from two different customer routers using two different customer ASNs (one is a backup connection from a secondary data center), and sets a lower MED on the primary path's advertisement. However, AWS continues to send traffic to the backup path more often than expected. What explains this?

choices.text: MED is only compared between routes received from the same neighboring AS; since the two connections use different customer ASNs, AWS does not compare their MED values against each other, so MED has no effect between them
MED values must be higher, not lower, to be preferred by AWS's BGP implementation
Direct Connect does not support MED on any virtual interface type
The backup path's route was learned via iBGP, so it is automatically preferred over the eBGP route on the primary path

explanation: The BGP best path algorithm compares MED only among routes from the same neighboring AS; with two different customer ASNs, AWS's routers cannot use MED to compare the paths, so selection falls through to other criteria. Lower MED is in fact preferred when comparable, DX does support standard BGP MED, and both Direct Connect BGP sessions are eBGP, not iBGP.

stem: A customer's on-premises router receives the same VPC prefix from AWS over two Direct Connect private VIFs: one path has a shorter AS path but the administrator manually set a lower local preference for it, while the other path has a longer AS path but a higher local preference. Which path does standard BGP best path selection choose?

choices.text: The path with the shorter AS path, because AS path length is always evaluated before local preference
The path with the higher local preference, because local preference is evaluated earlier in the standard BGP best path selection process than AS path length
Both paths are installed and traffic is load-balanced automatically since local preference and AS path conflict
Neither path is selected until MED is compared first, since MED precedes local preference

explanation: Standard BGP best path selection evaluates local preference before AS path length and well before MED, so a manually configured higher local preference overrides a shorter AS path on a competing route. BGP does not automatically load-balance across differing local preference or AS path values without explicit multipath configuration, and MED is evaluated after both local preference and AS path length.

stem: When configuring an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection with a customer gateway device that does not support BGP, which routing option must be used, and what is a key operational implication?

choices.text: Dynamic (BGP) routing must still be used; AWS Site-to-Site VPN does not support static routing

Static routing must be used, requiring the on-premises CIDR blocks to be manually specified for each tunnel, and failover between tunnels relies on the on-premises device detecting tunnel state rather than BGP route withdrawal
Static routing must be used, but failover between the two tunnels happens automatically at the AWS side with no on-premises configuration, identical to BGP
Policy-based VPN is required, and static or dynamic routing options do not apply to AWS Site-to-Site VPN

explanation: A customer gateway without BGP support requires static routing, where the administrator specifies on-premises prefixes per tunnel; since there is no BGP route withdrawal to signal a failure, the on-premises device must detect the tunnel-down condition (for example via IPsec dead peer detection) to fail over. AWS does support static routing, contradicting A and D, and failover is not fully automatic without proper on-premises detection, contradicting C.

stem: A Site-to-Site VPN connection using BGP dynamic routing has two tunnels, both showing UP status. During a planned maintenance test, the customer shuts down the primary tunnel's IPsec session on their firewall, but traffic does not fail over to the second tunnel for several minutes, causing an outage. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: The customer gateway is not promptly withdrawing the BGP route learned over the primary tunnel after the IPsec tunnel goes down, so the on-premises router keeps preferring the now-dead path
AWS Site-to-Site VPN does not support two tunnels being BGP-active simultaneously
The VPC route table's propagated routes cannot fail over without manual intervention
Both tunnels must terminate on the same on-premises device to support failover

explanation: BGP-based VPN failover depends on timely detection of tunnel failure and BGP route withdrawal (or hold-timer expiration) on the customer side; if the firewall delays withdrawing the route after the IPsec session drops, traffic keeps flowing to the dead tunnel until timers expire. AWS fully supports both tunnels being simultaneously active, VPC route table propagation updates automatically as BGP paths change, and tunnels need not terminate on the same device.

stem: A financial services company is deciding between static routing and BGP dynamic routing for a new Site-to-Site VPN that will back up an existing Direct Connect connection, and they plan to add and remove VPC CIDR ranges frequently as new workloads are deployed. Which tradeoff should most influence their decision toward BGP?

choices.text: BGP dynamic routing automatically propagates new or removed prefixes without requiring manual updates to static route entries on both sides each time the network changes
Static routing provides lower per-packet latency than BGP because it avoids the BGP control plane
BGP routing is required to enable AES-256 encryption on the VPN tunnels, while static routing is limited to AES-128
BGP dynamic routing is the only option that supports Equal-Cost Multi-Path across both tunnels

explanation: Given their frequent CIDR changes, the key operational advantage of BGP is that it dynamically advertises prefix changes, avoiding the manual route maintenance that static routing would require on every change. Encryption algorithm choice is independent of routing mode, latency is not materially affected by the BGP control plane's presence, and while ECMP is indeed BGP-only, it is not the tradeoff most relevant to their stated CIDR-churn problem.

stem: A healthcare company requires Direct Connect connectivity that can tolerate the failure of an entire Direct Connect location without manual intervention, and wants to meet AWS's defined resiliency model for that use case with the fewest connections possible. Which resiliency model should they choose?

choices.text: Development and Test model: one connection at one location
High Resiliency model: one connection at each of two different Direct Connect locations
Maximum Resiliency model: two connections at each of two different Direct Connect locations (four connections total)
A single Direct Connect connection using a LAG of two physical links at one location

explanation: The High Resiliency model uses two connections across two separate Direct Connect locations, protecting against the failure of an entire location using the minimum number of connections for that level of protection. Maximum Resiliency exceeds what is needed here by also protecting against a device failure, while Development/Test and a single-location LAG do not protect against a full location failure.

stem: A company believed it had implemented AWS's Maximum Resiliency model for Direct Connect by provisioning two connections, but an audit reveals both connections terminate on the same device at the same location through two separate ports. During a maintenance event on that device, both connections go down simultaneously. What was misconfigured relative to the Maximum Resiliency model?

choices.text: The connections should have been combined into a single LAG instead of kept separate
